claim: The gap gene system of dipteran insects is not structurally modular.
source: Here we partition an experimentally tractable regulatory network—the gap gene system of dipteran insects—using an alternative approach. We show that this system, although not structurally modular, is composed of dynamical modules driving different aspects of whole-network behaviour.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding based on the analysis presented in the paper.

claim: The gap gene system is composed of dynamical modules driving different aspects of whole-network behaviour.
source: We show that this system, although not structurally modular, is composed of dynamical modules driving different aspects of whole-network behaviour.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a main finding from the analysis.

claim: All dynamical modules in the gap gene system share the same regulatory structure but differ in components and sensitivity to regulatory interactions.
source: All these subcircuits share the same regulatory structure, but differ in components and sensitivity to regulatory interactions.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the analysis.

claim: Some subcircuits in the gap gene system are in a state of criticality while others are not.
source: Some subcircuits are in a state of criticality, while others are not, which explains the observed differential evolvability of the various expression features in the system.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a key finding from the bifurcation analysis.

claim: The differential criticality of subcircuits explains the observed differential evolvability of various expression features in the gap gene system.
source: Some subcircuits are in a state of criticality, while others are not, which explains the observed differential evolvability of the various expression features in the system.
evidence: The abstract presents this as an explanatory conclusion from the analysis.

claim: Structural modularity is widely regarded as a necessary condition for the evolvability of complex networks.
source: Structural modularity is widely regarded as a necessary condition for the evolvability of complex networks.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The most common strategy to identify functional modules is to partition the graph representing a network into simple motifs or subcircuits.
source: The most common strategy to identify functional modules is to partition the graph representing a network into simple motifs (Shen-Orr et al., 2002; Alon, 2007) or subcircuits (also called subnetworks or communities; (Girvan and Newman, 2002; Oliveri and Davidson, 2004; Babu et al., 2004; Levine and Davidson, 2005; Newman, 2006; Davidson and Erwin, 2006; Oliveri and Davidson, 2007; Erwin and Davidson, 2009; Davidson, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as common practice with supporting citations.

claim: Network motifs are small subgraphs that are identified through their statistical enrichment.
source: Network motifs are small subgraphs that are identified through their statistical enrichment (Alon, 2007; Alon, 2006)
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations.

claim: Subcircuits are characterised by a high connection density among their component nodes contrasting with sparse connections to the outside.
source: while subcircuits are characterised by a high connection density among their component nodes contrasting with sparse connections to the outside (Girvan and Newman, 2002; Radicchi et al., 2004; Newman, 2006; Wagner et al., 2007; Fortunato, 2010).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations.

claim: The gap gene network reads and interprets morphogen gradients formed along the antero-posterior axis of the embryo by the protein products of maternal co-ordinate genes bicoid, caudal, and hunchback.
source: The gap gene network reads and interprets morphogen gradients formed along the major or antero-posterior (A–P) axis of the embryo by the protein products of the maternal co-ordinate genes bicoid (bcd), caudal (cad), and hunchback (hb).
evidence: This describes the biological function of the gap gene network.

claim: The gap gene network produces broad, overlapping expression domains for the trunk gap genes hb, Krüppel, knirps, and giant.
source: This results in broad, overlapping expression domains for the trunk gap genes hb, Krüppel (Kr), knirps (kni), and giant (gt) (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B, C.

claim: Extensive gap-gene cross-regulation during cleavage cycle 14A is essential for the correct dynamic positioning of expression domain boundaries.
source: Extensive gap-gene cross-regulation, especially during the last cleavage cycle (cycle 14A, C14A) of the blastoderm stage, is essential for the correct dynamic positioning of expression domain boundaries, in particular the dynamic kinematic shifts of posterior gap domains towards the anterior of the embryo (Jaeger et al., 2004b; Jaeger et al., 2004a; Surkova et al., 2008; Manu et al., 2009a; Crombach et al., 2012; Verd et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding with supporting citations.

claim: Due to its small size and high connection density, it is not possible to identify structural clusters in the gap gene system.
source: Due to its small size and high connection density (see Figure 1A), it is not possible to identify structural clusters in the gap gene system.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the network structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The gap gene network contains two double-negative (positive) feedback loops between hb/kni and Kr/gt that are responsible for the basic staggered arrangement of gap domains along the A–P axis.
source: One of these consists of two double-negative (positive) feedback loops between hb/kni and Kr/gt that are responsible for the basic staggered arrangement of gap domains along the A–P axis.
evidence: This is stated as a previously identified mechanism with supporting citations.

claim: Asymmetric repressive interactions between overlapping gap genes drive dynamic anterior shifts of gap domains over time.
source: Another one comprises the asymmetric repressive interactions between overlapping gap genes (e. g. kni on Kr and Kr on hb) that are driving dynamic anterior shifts of gap domains over time (Figure 1A, B) (Jaeger et al., 2004a; Jaeger et al., 2004b; Jaeger, 2011; Crombach et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a previously identified mechanism with supporting citations and illustrated in Figure 1A, B.

claim: Attempts to explain gap gene expression dynamics with network motifs have consistently failed to correctly account for the integrated behaviour of the whole system.
source: Moreover, attempts to explain gap gene expression dynamics with network motifs have consistently failed to correctly account for the integrated behaviour of the whole system (Zinzen and Papatsenko, 2007; Ishihara and Shibata, 2008; Papatsenko, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from previous studies with supporting citations.

claim: The gap gene network is a strongly emergent network.
source: All these difficulties arise because the gap gene network is a strongly emergent network (sensu Jiménez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of the network based on the definition from Jiménez et al., 2017.

claim: Most functionally modular networks are not modular in the strict structural sense.
source: Most networks identified by the screen fell somewhere in between these two extremes, that is, they show partial structural overlap between functional modules. This suggests that most functionally modular networks are not modular in the strict structural sense.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the computational screen by Jiménez et al., 2017.

claim: Dynamical modules consist of a group of connected network nodes that implement a particular behaviour.
source: Such dynamical modules or dynamical subsystems consist of a group of connected network nodes that implement a particular behaviour (Irons and Monk, 2007; Benítez and Alvarez-Buylla, 2010).
evidence: This is a definition of dynamical modules with supporting citations.

claim: The spatio-temporal pattern of activity of dynamical modules specifies a certain type of dynamics termed a 'dynamical regime'.
source: Their spatio-temporal pattern of activity specifies a certain type of dynamics—such as bistable or oscillatory—termed a 'dynamical regime' (Verd et al., 2017; Verd et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a definition with supporting citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: Different dynamical regimes are distinguished by the composition of the underlying phase portraits.
source: Different dynamical regimes are distinguished by the composition of the underlying phase portraits (Strogatz, 2015; Perez-Carrasco et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of dynamical regimes with supporting citations.

claim: Dynamical modules are not the same as co-expression modules.
source: Note that dynamical modules are not the same as co-expression modules (sometimes also called regulatory modules; see, for example, Eisen et al., 1998; Bar-Joseph et al., 2003; Segal et al., 2003; Stuart et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2009; Koch et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a clarification with supporting citations.

claim: Co-expression modules are defined by the correlated or anti-correlated expression of their components.
source: The latter are defined by the correlated or anti-correlated expression of their components.
evidence: This is a definition of co-expression modules.

claim: The mutual dependence of component expression patterns in dynamical modules is causal, rather than correlative.
source: In contrast, the mutual dependence of component expression patterns in dynamical modules is causal, rather than correlative.
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing characteristic of dynamical modules.

claim: Dynamical modules are identified by the coherent collective activity of the module as a whole.
source: Dynamical modules are not identified by individual expression patterns, but rather by the coherent collective activity of the module as a whole (Kauffman, 1993; Irons and Monk, 2007; Alexander et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a defining characteristic with supporting citations.

claim: Some dynamical modules may be in a state of criticality, close to a bifurcation point, while others may be structurally stable.
source: In particular, some dynamical modules may be in a state of criticality, close to a bifurcation point beyond which their dynamics may change drastically and abruptly; others may be structurally stable, that is, not critical and far from any bifurcation, and therefore insensitive or robust to changes in parameters (Thom, 1976; Kauffman, 1993; Jaeger et al., 2012; Jaeger and Monk, 2014; Jaeger and Sharpe, 2014; Strogatz, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of dynamical modules with supporting citations.

claim: Mutations affecting network components involved in multiple dynamical regimes will tend to have a strong effect on critical behaviours while leaving structurally stable behaviours unaltered.
source: Mutations affecting these components will tend to have a strong effect on those behaviours that are critical, leaving others unaltered because they are structurally stable.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of differential criticality in dynamical modules.

claim: The gap gene system can be reduced from four to three trunk gap genes in three distinct regions of the embryo.
source: Therefore, the gap gene regulatory network can be reduced from four to three trunk gap genes in each of these three regions (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the node sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Between 35 and 47% A-P position, developmental trajectories are insensitive to kni.
source: (1 in the region between 35 and 47% A–P position, developmental trajectories are insensitive to kni (red background)
evidence: This is stated as a result from the node sensitivity analysis.

claim: Between 49 and 59% A-P position, developmental trajectories are insensitive to gt.
source: (2) between 49 and 59% A–P position, they are insensitive to gt (blue)
evidence: This is stated as a result from the node sensitivity analysis.

claim: Between 61 and 75% A-P position, developmental trajectories are insensitive to hb.
source: (3) between 61 and 75% A–P position, they are insensitive to hb (yellow).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the node sensitivity analysis.

claim: All three AC/DC subcircuits identified in the gap gene system share the same regulatory structure.
source: Surprisingly, the structure of all three resulting subcircuits is qualitatively the same, even though each involves a different (overlapping set of gap genes (Figure 2B), and therefore distinct strengths of regulatory interactions (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis and shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The AC/DC circuit structure combines a negative feedback loop between all three genes with a double-negative (positive) feedback loop between two of them.
source: This structure combines a negative feedback loop between all three genes of a subcircuit with a double-negative (positive) feedback loop between two of them (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the AC/DC structure and shown in Figure 2B, C.

claim: The AC/DC circuit was first described in the context of dorso-ventral patterning in the vertebrate neural tube.
source: Such a combination between positive and negative feedback loops is called the 'AC/DC circuit,' first described in the context of dorso-ventral patterning in the vertebrate neural tube (Balaskas et al., 2012; Panovska-Griffiths et al., 2013; Perez-Carrasco et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as background information with supporting citations.

claim: Strong positive feedback is required for the basic staggered arrangement of gap domains.
source: Previous work has shown that strong positive feedback is required for the basic staggered arrangement of gap domains ('alternating cushions'), while weaker (and hence slower) negative feedback drives anterior shifts in gap domain position over time in the posterior trunk region of the embryo (Jaeger et al., 2004b; Jaeger et al., 2004a; Perkins et al., 2006; Ashyraliyev et al., 2009; Jaeger, 2011; Crombach et al., 2012; Verd et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding from previous work with supporting citations.

claim: Weaker negative feedback drives anterior shifts in gap domain position over time in the posterior trunk region of the embryo.
source: Previous work has shown that strong positive feedback is required for the basic staggered arrangement of gap domains ('alternating cushions'), while weaker (and hence slower) negative feedback drives anterior shifts in gap domain position over time in the posterior trunk region of the embryo (Jaeger et al., 2004b; Jaeger et al., 2004a; Perkins et al., 2006; Ashyraliyev et al., 2009; Jaeger, 2011; Crombach et al., 2012; Verd et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding from previous work with supporting citations.

claim: All three AC/DC subcircuits reproduce the expression dynamics of the full model with reasonable accuracy in their respective regions of influence throughout cleavage cycle 14A.
source: All three AC/DC subcircuits—AC/DC1 in the anterior, AC/DC2 in the middle, and AC/DC3 in the posterior—reproduce the expression dynamics of the full model with reasonable accuracy in their respective regions of influence throughout cleavage cycle 14A, which we subdivide into eight time classes T1–8 of equal length for the purpose of our analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Jaeger et al., 2004b; Jaeger et al., 2004a; Surkova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The anterior boundary of the posterior gt domain fails to shift in the AC/DC3 model, starting to deviate from the full model around time class T3.
source: The only major expression defect involves the anterior boundary of the posterior gt domain, which fails to shift in the AC/DC3 model, starting to deviate from the full model around time class T3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observed defect in the AC/DC3 model and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: AC/DC1 consists of nodes representing hb, Kr, and gt and its region of influence lies between 35 and 47% A–P position.
source: AC/DC1 consists of nodes representing hb, Kr, and gt (Figure 2C, left panel. Its region of influence lies between 35 and 47% A–P position (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as a description of AC/DC1 and shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: Phase portraits of AC/DC1 exhibit multistability with two or more point attractors.
source: Phase portraits in this region exhibit multistability with two or more point attractors (shown for the nucleus at 37% A–P position in Figure 3B, left; additional nuclei are shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated as a result from phase space analysis and shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Trajectories of AC/DC1 are very similar to those simulated with the full model.
source: These trajectories are very similar to those simulated with the full model, suggesting that flow direction and magnitude is conserved between both models (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplements 2A, A').
evidence: This is stated as a result from phase space analysis and shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplements 2A, A'.

claim: AC/DC2 consists of nodes representing hb, Kr, and kni and is active between 49 and 59% A–P position.
source: The nodes in AC/DC2 represent hb, Kr, and kni (Figure 2C, central panel), and it is active between 49 and 59% A–P position (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as a description of AC/DC2 and shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: AC/DC2's region of influence straddles the bifurcation that occurs at 52% A–P position in the full model.
source: This region straddles the bifurcation that occurs at 52% A–P position in the full model, designating the division between static anterior and shifting posterior gap domains (Manu et al., 2009a; Gursky et al., 2011; Verd et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of AC/DC2's region with supporting citations.

claim: The phase portrait of AC/DC2 at 49% A-P position is bistable for all time points except the last one.
source: The phase portrait of AC/DC2 in this nucleus is bistable for all time points except the last one (at T8, when it becomes monostable and only an attractor close to the origin persists (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated as a result from phase space analysis and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Posterior to the bifurcation at 52% A–P position, the full model exhibits trajectories that curve towards a spiral sink attractor in a monostable phase portrait.
source: Posterior to the bifurcation at 52% A–P position, the full model exhibits trajectories that curve towards a spiral sink attractor in a monostable phase portrait (Verd et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the full model with a supporting citation.

claim: The trajectories of AC/DC2 posterior to the bifurcation are very similar to those of the full model.
source: The trajectories of AC/DC2 in this region are very similar (Figure 3B for the nucleus at 59% A–P position, see Figure 3—figure supplements 2B, B' for trajectories in other nuclei).
evidence: This is stated as a result from phase space analysis and shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplements 2B, B'.

claim: The underlying topology of phase space is not equivalent in the AC/DC2 subcircuit and the full model posterior to the bifurcation.
source: Interestingly, however, the underlying topology of phase space is not equivalent in the AC/DC2 subcircuit and the full model.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from phase space analysis.

claim: There are no spiral sinks in AC/DC2 posterior to the bifurcation, with spiral sinks appearing only late at time points T7 and T8.
source: While both models exhibit monostability in this region, and trajectories in both are shaped by the pursuit of a moving attractor, there are no spiral sinks in AC/DC2 (Figure 3B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B). Spiralling trajectories in this subcircuit are shaped mainly by the movement of a conventional point attractor, with spiral sinks appearing only late, at time points T7 and T8.
evidence: This is stated as a result from phase space analysis and shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Identical transient behaviour can be caused by different types of moving attractors in time-variant or non-autonomous dynamical systems.
source: This illustrates that identical transient behaviour can be caused by different types of moving attractors in (biological) time-variant or non-autonomous dynamical systems.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the phase space analysis.

claim: AC/DC3 consists of nodes representing Kr, kni, and gt and is active between 61 and 75% A–P position.
source: The nodes in AC/DC3 represent Kr, kni, and gt (Figure 2C, right panel). It is active between 61 and 75% A–P position (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as a description of AC/DC3 and shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: AC/DC3 faithfully reproduces the dynamics of gap gene expression obtained from the full model in nuclei at 61 and 63% A–P position.
source: In the nuclei at 61 and 63% A–P position, AC/DC3 faithfully reproduces the dynamics of gap gene expression obtained from the full model (Figure 3B, right, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the analysis and shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Posterior to 63% A–P position, AC/DC3 no longer recapitulates gap gene expression dynamics accurately.
source: Posterior to 63% A–P position, AC/DC3 no longer recapitulates gap gene expression dynamics accurately, because its trajectories fail to switch from the Kr-Kni to the Kni-Gt plane as they do in the full model (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: AC/DC subcircuits are true dynamical modules of the gap gene network in the region between 35% and 63% A–P position.
source: In summary, phase space analysis of AC/DC subcircuits establishes that they are true dynamical modules of the gap gene network in the region between 35% and 63% A–P position (Irons and Monk, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the phase space analysis with a supporting citation.

claim: AC/DC subcircuits faithfully recover the geometry of trajectories in the full model.
source: They faithfully recover the geometry of trajectories in the full model, whose phase portrait can be seen as an overlapping composite of those of the subcircuits in this region.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the phase space analysis.

claim: AC/DC1 and AC/DC3 each have a consistent dynamical regime across their respective regions of influence.
source: AC/DC1 in the anterior and AC/DC3 in the posterior each have a consistent dynamical regime across their respective regions of influence (Figures 1–3), indicating that these two dynamical modules are structurally stable with respect to inputs from maternal gradients.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figures 1–3.

claim: AC/DC1 and AC/DC3 are structurally stable with respect to inputs from maternal gradients.
source: AC/DC1 in the anterior and AC/DC3 in the posterior each have a consistent dynamical regime across their respective regions of influence (Figures 1–3), indicating that these two dynamical modules are structurally stable with respect to inputs from maternal gradients.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figures 1–3.

claim: AC/DC2 correctly reproduces the bifurcation observed in the full model at 52% A–P position.
source: In contrast, AC/DC2 correctly reproduces the bifurcation observed in the full model at 52% A–P position, which separates static anterior patterning from kinematically shifting domains in the posterior (Figure 3) (Manu et al., 2009a; Gursky et al., 2011; Verd et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the analysis shown in Figure 3 with supporting citations.

claim: AC/DC2 is in a state of criticality with respect to the inputs from maternal gradients.
source: The presence of a bifurcation implies that this dynamical module is in a state of criticality with respect to the inputs from maternal gradients.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the observation of the bifurcation.

claim: The gap gene network of D. melanogaster is critical to maternal inputs only in the middle of the embryo, where AC/DC2 is active between 49 and 59% A–P position.
source: Our analysis therefore suggests that the gap gene network of D. melanogaster is critical to maternal inputs only in the middle of the embryo, where AC/DC2 is active between 49 and 59% A–P position, while it is structurally stable outside of this region.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: Gap gene patterning in the central region of the D. melanogaster blastoderm is robust towards variation in the levels of maternal gradients.
source: For instance, gap gene patterning in the central region of the D. melanogaster blastoderm is robust towards variation in the levels of maternal gradients (Figure 4) (Houchmandzadeh et al., 2002; Gregor et al., 2007a; Manu et al., 2009b; Gursky et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding with supporting citations and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The position of the bifurcation boundary between static and shifting gap domains is labile between different dipteran species.
source: In contrast, the position of the bifurcation boundary between static and shifting gap domains is labile between different dipteran species (Jaeger et al., 2004b; Surkova et al., 2008; Manu et al., 2009a; García-Solache et al., 2010; Jaeger, 2011; Crombach et al., 2014; Wotton et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding with supporting citations.

claim: In the scuttle fly Megaselia abdita, the bifurcation boundary is located more anteriorly compared to D. melanogaster.
source: In the scuttle fly Megaselia abdita (Phoridae), it is located more anteriorly compared to D. melanogaster: the region where gap domain shifts occur includes the Hb-Kr interface at around 40% A–P position (see Figure 5 below) (Wotton et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The moth midge Clogmia albipunctata shows even more extended and pronounced gap domain shifts than D. melanogaster.
source: The moth midge Clogmia albipunctata (Psychodidae) shows even more extended and pronounced gap domain shifts (García-Solache et al., 2010; Crombach et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting citations.

claim: There is a threshold response in AC/DC2 at a Bcd concentration of approximately 15 arbitrary units.
source: The resulting dynamical regimes are shown in the phase diagram displayed in Figure 4B. There is a threshold response at a Bcd concentration of approximately 15 arbitrary units: above this threshold, the system is bistable; below, it is monostable.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the phase diagram analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Bcd concentrations in nuclei anterior of 52% fall into the multistable regime, while nuclei posterior of this position fall into the monostable regime.
source: Bcd concentrations in nuclei anterior of 52% fall into the multistable regime, nuclei posterior of this position fall into the monostable regime (see dots in Figure 4B), recovering the same bifurcation position as in the full model (Manu et al., 2009a; Gursky et al., 2011; Verd et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the phase diagram analysis shown in Figure 4B with supporting citations.

claim: The position of the bifurcation boundary in AC/DC2 is entirely insensitive to Cad concentration.
source: The resulting phase diagram shows that, in contrast to Bcd, the position of the bifurcation boundary is entirely insensitive to Cad concentration. There is an abrupt vertical divide between dynamical regimes around 52% A–P position (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the phase diagram analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Varying Cad concentration has no effect on the position of the bifurcation and therefore the extent of the posterior region that exhibits dynamic gap domain shifts.
source: This implies that varying Cad concentration has no effect on the position of the bifurcation, and therefore the extent of the posterior region that exhibits dynamic gap domain shifts.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the phase diagram analysis.

claim: Cad serves as a general activator in the posterior but is not directly involved in setting the position of gap gene expression features.
source: This complements earlier studies which suggested that Cad serves as a general activator in the posterior, but is not directly involved in setting the position of gap gene expression features (Struhl et al., 1992; Manu et al., 2009a; Verd et al., 2017), or in controlling the rate of gap domain shifts in this region of the embryo (Verd et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion that complements earlier studies with supporting citations.

claim: In M. abdita, the anterior localization domain of bcd mRNA is expanded compared to D. melanogaster, which presumably leads to an expanded Bcd protein gradient.
source: In this species, the anterior localization domain of bcd mRNA is expanded compared to D. melanogaster, which presumably leads to an expanded Bcd protein gradient (Stauber et al., 1999; Stauber et al., 2000; Wotton et al., 2015; Crombach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting citations.

claim: Despite more Bcd being present in M. abdita, the bifurcation boundary is located further anterior than in D. melanogaster.
source: However, despite more Bcd being present, the bifurcation boundary is located further anterior than in D. melanogaster (Figure 5A) (Wotton et al., 2015; Crombach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting citations and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The strength of gap-gap cross-regulatory interactions differs between M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: Previous studies have shown that the strength of gap-gap cross-regulatory interactions differs between M. abdita and D. melanogaster (Wotton et al., 2015; Crombach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding with supporting citations.

claim: In D. melanogaster, repression of hb by Kr is negligible.
source: In our D. melanogaster model, repression of hb by Kr is negligible (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the D. melanogaster model shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In M. abdita, there is a significant net repressive effect of Kr on hb.
source: In contrast, both genetic evidence (Wotton et al., 2015) and models (Crombach et al., 2016) for M. abdita indicate that there is a significant net repressive effect of Kr on hb in this species.
evidence: This is stated as an established finding with supporting citations.

claim: If repression of hb by Kr remains minimal in AC/DC2, the bifurcation occurs at 52% A–P position.
source: If repression remains minimal (closer to zero than −0.0005), we recover the bifurcation at 52% A–P position, as nuclei anterior to this position are multistable, while more posterior nuclei are monostable (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the phase diagram analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: If the strength of repression of hb by Kr is increased in AC/DC2, the bifurcation boundary moves anteriorly and vanishes altogether around a repression strength of −0.0025.
source: If the strength of repression is further increased, the bifurcation boundary moves anteriorly and vanishes altogether around a repression strength of −0.0025.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the phase diagram analysis.

claim: The position of the bifurcation boundary in AC/DC2 is largely insensitive to the interaction between kni and Kr.
source: In contrast, the position of the bifurcation boundary is largely insensitive to the interaction between kni and Kr (Figure 5, D).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the phase diagram analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: AC/DC2 in M. abdita should be structurally stable, as net repression of hb by Kr is increased in this species.
source: Taken together, the analysis predicts that AC/DC2 in M. abdita should be structurally stable, as net repression of hb by Kr is increased in this species (Wotton et al., 2015; Crombach et al., 2016), eliminating the bifurcation boundary present in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the analysis with supporting citations.

claim: Increasing the strength of repression of hb by Kr does not induce a bifurcation in AC/DC1.
source: Interestingly, this is not the case, as AC/DC1 remains multistable regardless of repression strength due to the very strong positive feedback between Kr and gt (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the phase diagram analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: At least two repressive interactions must be stronger in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster to render AC/DC1 critical in this species.
source: Therefore, at least two repressive interactions must be stronger in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster to render AC/DC1 critical in this species.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the phase diagram analysis.

claim: In D. melanogaster only AC/DC2 is critical, while in M. abdita the bifurcation boundary between static and dynamic patterning regimes falls into the region of influence of AC/DC1.
source: In summary, our analysis suggests that in D. melanogaster only AC/DC2 is critical, while in M. abdita the bifurcation boundary between static and dynamic patterning regimes falls into the region of influence of AC/DC1.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: The change in the stability of dynamical modules between D. melanogaster and M. abdita is caused by changes in the strength of particular gap-gap cross-repressive interactions.
source: This change in the stability of dynamical modules is caused by changes in the strength of particular gap-gap cross-repressive interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: Small changes in the strength of gap-gap cross-regulatory interactions specifically affect the extent of static versus shifting patterning regimes.
source: Our work predicts that small changes in the strength of gap-gap cross-regulatory interactions specifically affect the extent of static versus shifting patterning regimes.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the analysis.

claim: The basic staggered arrangement of domain boundaries remains remarkably stable during the evolution of cyclorrhaphan flies.
source: In contrast, other aspects of gap gene patterning, such as the alternating-cushions mechanism of positive feedback between Kr and gt as well as hb and kni, are extremely robust towards changes in interaction strengths.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: Diffusion of gap proteins is not essential for pattern formation in the gap gene system.
source: Earlier studies have established that diffusion of gap proteins is not essential for pattern formation (Jaeger et al., 2004b; Manu et al., 2009a; Verd et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding with supporting citations.

claim: The full gap gene model accurately reproduces the spatio-temporal expression dynamics of gap gene expression.
source: The circuit used here is identical to that published and described in Verd et al. (2017); Verd et al. (2018). It accurately reproduces the spatio-temporal expression dynamics of gap gene expression (see Figure 1B), and is fully consistent with the available experimental evidence on gap gene regulation (see Jaeger et al., 2004b; Jaeger et al., 2004a; Manu et al., 2009b; Manu et al., 2009a; Ashyraliyev et al., 2009; Jaeger, 2011; Crombach et al., 2012; Verd et al., 2017; Verd et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a validation of the model with supporting citations and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The full gap gene model is fully consistent with the available experimental evidence on gap gene regulation.
source: It accurately reproduces the spatio-temporal expression dynamics of gap gene expression (see Figure 1B), and is fully consistent with the available experimental evidence on gap gene regulation (see Jaeger et al., 2004b; Jaeger et al., 2004a; Manu et al., 2009b; Manu et al., 2009a; Ashyraliyev et al., 2009; Jaeger, 2011; Crombach et al., 2012; Verd et al., 2017; Verd et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a validation of the model with supporting citations.

claim: AC/DC circuits can be induced to drive sustained limit-cycle oscillations with relatively small additional changes in the values of parameters that determine cross-regulatory interactions.
source: An extended analysis of our AC/DC circuits (see Appendix 1) reveals that they can be induced to drive sustained limit-cycle oscillations with relatively small additional changes in the values of parameters that determine cross-regulatory interactions (summarized in Figure 6) (Panovska-Griffiths et al., 2013; Perez-Carrasco et al., 2018; Page and Perez-Carrasco, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the extended analysis shown in Figure 6 with supporting citations.

claim: Gap genes in T. castaneum show repeated waves of kinematically shifting gene expression in the blastoderm and germband of the embryo.
source: Although gap genes do not seem to be directly involved in the process of segment determination in T. castaneum, they do show repeated waves of kinematically shifting gene expression in the blastoderm and germband of the embryo (Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a supporting citation.

claim: Pair-rule genes in T. castaneum are known to be essential for segment determination in all arthropods.
source: So do pair-rule genes (Sarrazin et al., 2012; El-Sherif et al., 2012; El-Sherif et al., 2014), which are known to be essential for segment determination in all arthropods.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Pair-rule genes in T. castaneum may be regulated by AC/DC-like regulatory subcircuits.
source: Pair-rule genes in T. castaneum may also be regulated by AC/DC-like regulatory subcircuits (Choe et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as a possibility with a supporting citation.

claim: The regulatory changes required to turn sequential (short-germband) into simultaneous (long-germband) segmentation may be much more subtle than commonly thought.
source: These surprising resemblances suggest that ancestral gap and pair-rule expression may have relied on similar regulatory principles, and that the regulatory changes required to turn sequential (short-germband) into simultaneous (long-germband) segmentation may be much more subtle than commonly thought (see Tautz, 2004; Clark, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on the analysis with supporting citations.

claim: Most regulatory networks are of emergent rather than hybrid type, exhibiting dynamical but not necessarily structural modularity.
source: The in silico screen performed by Jiménez et al. (2017) suggests that many regulatory systems are capable of multistable behaviours, while different dynamical regimes rarely map to cleanly separable clusters in the structure of the network. In other words, most regulatory networks are of emergent rather than hybrid type, exhibiting dynamical but not necessarily structural modularity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the computational screen by Jiménez et al., 2017.

claim: Dynamical behaviour is much more tightly integrated with biological function than the regulatory structure of a network.
source: They bring us closer to the aim of identifying true functional modules in evolving developmental systems (Wagner, 2014), as dynamical behaviour is much more tightly integrated with biological function than the regulatory structure of a network.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with a supporting citation.
